notes.wange: Agrees with the noun: maama wangye, ekitabo kyangye, ebitabo byangye.
notes.jjajja: Nyakuru is a grandmother; a grandfather is shwenkuru.
notes.emmere: Ebyokurya, literally “things for eating”, is plural: ebyokurya ni birungi.
notes.omusomesa: From -egyesa, to teach; omwegi (student) is from -ega, to learn.
notes.kaka: Mwene waitu, “the child of ours”, is any sibling.
notes.dada: A man’s sister. Between sisters, people say mwene waitu.
notes.wake: We agrees with omu- nouns: maama we, his or her mother.
notes.huyu: Ogu for people and omu- nouns: ogu ni maama wangye.

guidebook.intro: Runyankore sorts nouns into classes, each with its own prefix. The prefix tells you how to make the plural and how “my” must change to match.

tips.title: Noun classes: omu-/aba-, eki-/ebi-
body: People take **omu-** in the singular and **aba-** in the plural: **omuntu, abantu**; **omushaija, abashaija**. Many things take **eki-** and **ebi-**: **ekitabo, ebitabo**.
Words that go with a noun copy its class: **ekitabo kyangye** (my book) but **ebitabo byangye** (my books).

tips.title: Ni-: what I’m doing now
body: Everyday actions start with **ni-** and the person: **n-** for “I”, **o-** for “you”. **Ninda** (I eat), **Ninywa** (I drink), **Ninsoma** (I read), **Noyenda ki?** (what do you want?).
The verb **-enda** (want, like) is used for both: **Ninyenda amaizi** (I want water).

culture.title: Family is wide
body: Your father’s brothers are also your fathers, and your mother’s sisters are your mothers. Cousins are often called brothers and sisters: **mwene waitu**, literally “the child of ours”.
